planting.note: Plant rooted pad cuttings in spring in gravelly, alkaline, fast-draining soil in full sun once the pads have callused for several days.

directions: Cinnamon pricklypear is a Chihuahuan Desert native prized for its rounded gray-green pads and dense, velvety, rust-colored glochid patches instead of true spines, which give the plant a warm cinnamon-brown glow in strong sunlight. Small yellow flowers open along the pad margins in late spring, followed by reddish-purple fruit that persists into fall. Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or rocky alkaline soil and withhold water almost entirely once established, since it is highly drought-adapted and prone to rot in heavy or poorly drained ground. Although the plant lacks large spines, the glochids detach on contact and irritate skin readily, so handle pads with thick gloves and tongs.

planting.note: Root pad cuttings in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; this species eventually forms a small, sprawling tree and needs room to spread.

directions: Native to South America and now naturalized in warm regions worldwide, drooping prickly pear develops a woody trunk over time and holds its long, thin, glossy green pads at a distinctive downward angle, giving mature plants a tree-like, weeping silhouette unlike most clumping Opuntia. It bears bright yellow flowers in late spring followed by red-purple fruit, and single sharp spines are scattered sparsely across otherwise smooth pads. Grow in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, and protect from hard freezes since it is noticeably less cold-hardy than most cold-climate prickly pears. Because it can self-sow and naturalize aggressively in frost-free climates, site it where spread can be managed or contained.

planting.note: Pot up rooted offsets in spring in fast-draining cactus mix in full sun to bright light; this species clusters readily and can be divided as it multiplies.

directions: A small globose cactus native to Guanajuato, Mexico, Zeilmann's pincushion is covered in fine white radial spines and slender hooked central spines, and it produces an eye-catching ring of vivid magenta-purple flowers around its crown in late spring. It offsets freely from the base, quickly forming a tight cluster of multiple heads that can be separated and repotted to propagate new plants. Grow in bright light or full sun with excellent drainage, watering only once the soil has dried completely, since it is highly susceptible to rot in cool, damp conditions. Keep frost-free year-round, bringing containers indoors well before the first fall cold snap.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant offsets or young plants in spring in gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in full sun; older colonies benefit from a slightly larger, shallow container to accommodate spreading mounds.

directions: Twin-spine cactus takes its common name from the paired long central spines that arise from each dense cushion of shorter white radial spines, giving the whole plant a snowy, bristling appearance broken by a crown of small magenta-pink flowers in a springtime ring. Native to central Mexico, individual columnar stems slowly clump into wide, mounded colonies of dozens of heads over many years, making it a rewarding long-term container or rock-garden specimen in frost-free climates. Provide full sun, sharply drained gritty soil, and infrequent deep watering only once the mix has dried out completely. Protect from prolonged cold, wet conditions, which cause rot far more readily than cold alone.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Pot rooted offsets in spring in gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in full sun; this species branches from the base with age to form small clumps.

directions: Owl-eye pincushion cactus is named for its paired, dark-tipped central spines that sit close together atop each areole, resembling a pair of watchful eyes against the plant's dense white spine coverage. Native to Queretaro and Hidalgo in central Mexico, it bears small cream to pale yellow flowers with a fine reddish midstripe in spring, followed by slender pink fruit. It branches at the base as it matures, gradually forming a modest clump of columnar stems rather than a single specimen. Grow in full sun with gritty, sharply drained soil and let the mix dry out fully between waterings, since it is intolerant of cold, soggy conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Start from divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun to preserve the strain's high essential-oil content, since seed-grown plants vary widely in pungency.

directions: Native to the mountains of central and eastern Anatolia in Turkey, this species is one of several wild oreganos harvested regionally for the dried-herb trade known locally as kekik, valued for its notably high concentration of aromatic oils compared to many garden oregano species. Its narrow, pointed leaves and pale pink to white summer flower spikes are smaller and more delicate-looking than common Greek oregano, but the dried leaf carries a robust, resinous, peppery bite. Grow in lean, rocky or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun, mimicking its native hillside habitat, and avoid rich, moisture-retentive beds that dilute flavor and invite root rot. Harvest just before flowering for the most concentrated essential-oil content, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; propagate vegetatively to keep the cream-and-pink variegated foliage true.

directions: Polyphant is a UK-raised ornamental oregano selection grown chiefly for its striking young foliage, which emerges cream-white and gradually flushes soft pink at the leaf margins before settling toward gray-green, giving the plant a long season of color interest well before the pale pink summer flower clusters appear. It forms a tidy, low mound and is best used at the front of a border, in a rock garden, or trailing over a container edge where the variegation can be appreciated up close. Provide lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich or damp conditions weaken the variegation and encourage rot. Shear back after flowering to keep growth compact and to encourage fresh, brightly variegated new foliage.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions after the last hard frost in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; this hybrid oregano is grown for its trailing hop-like flower bracts rather than culinary use.

directions: Barbara Tingey is a hardy ornamental oregano hybrid grown for its cascading clusters of overlapping chartreuse-green bracts that blush dusky pink-purple as they mature, resembling small dangling hops held above aromatic gray-green foliage. Compared with the similar but more tender Kent Beauty, this selection is generally considered more vigorous and better able to shrug off winter wet in temperate gardens. It suits a raised bed, dry stone wall, or container where its trailing stems can spill over an edge and be viewed from below. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid heavy, waterlogged ground, which quickly causes crown rot in humid or wet winters.
